metadata.title: Do parents of 15-year-olds know many of their child’s school friends and their parents? (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus brief uses OECD’s PISA 2015 database and reports descriptive comparisons and associations across countries/economies that distributed the parent questionnaire. The excerpt does not specify whether student sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the reported estimates, so the weighting approach cannot be confirmed from the provided text. For analysts working with PISA microdata, complex survey design weights should be used to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the stratified/clustered sampling design. The brief also does not describe any plausible-value (PV) or scaling model re-estimation; therefore, users should rely on the official PISA scoring and PV procedures for the relevant cognitive domain outcomes (e.g., collaborative problem solving) when reproducing results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The document reports PISA results (e.g., collaborative problem solving and bullying experiences) and parent acquaintances, but it does not provide methodological details on plausible-value generation/combining or any explicit missing-data handling procedure. This is best treated as a reporting gap for missing-data strategy because the brief does not describe whether missing questionnaire responses were excluded, imputed, or handled via PISA’s standard procedures. Since the provided text is a short policy brief rather than a full technical methods paper, the PV and missing-data workflow is not documented here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief restricts the displayed comparisons to the subset of PISA 2015 countries and economies that distributed the parent questionnaire (“Only countries and economies that distributed the parent questionnaire are shown”). It reports parent acquaintances at school based on parent responses to two items: number of the child’s school friends known by name and number of the friends’ parents known at the child’s school. For the bullying and collaborative problem solving associations, the brief further conditions on students’ socio-economic status (and reports results “after accounting for socio-economic status”), but it does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., complete-case requirements, missing-response thresholds, or PV-based analytic sample restrictions) in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief uses PISA 2015 data and focuses on parents’ social connectedness at school, measured as how many of their child’s school friends they know by name and how many of those friends’ parents they know. Across OECD education systems that distributed the parent questionnaire, parents reported knowing about five school friends and four friends’ parents on average, with large cross-country differences (e.g., higher in Georgia, Ireland and Spain; lower in Hong Kong (China), Korea and Macao (China)). The brief reports that students whose parents knew more of their friends and friends’ parents scored higher in collaborative problem solving and reported fewer bullying experiences, even after accounting for students’ socio-economic status. It also links higher parent acquaintances to greater attendance at parent meetings/conferences, suggesting that opportunities for school-community interaction may support intergenerational closure. The document explicitly notes that PISA cannot prove cause and effect, and it does not provide technical details on PV handling or missing-data procedures in the excerpt.
